title: Mattuck Brook (East Moriches)
summary: Mattuck is a recorded East Moriches brook name used as the eastern boundary of Watchogue Neck. Tooker's 1911 interpretation—“bad creek”—is explicitly uncertain, and the surrounding records also preserve a 1679 land purchase and Mayhue's 1680 reference to his kinsman Warishone living west of Watchogue.
activity_update_summary: Added a cited introduction connecting the Mattuck brook name to Watchogue's recorded boundaries, Tooker's uncertain interpretation, the 1677–1679 purchase record, and Mayhue's 1680 reference to his kinsman Warishone; corrected the displayed source pages and linked the existing Historic Moments.
why_this_matters: Mattuck is more than a proposed translation. The name connects a brook, neighboring waterways, a land purchase, and the home of Mayhue's kinsman Warishone, remembered in a 1680 deed. Reading those records together keeps kinship and residence visible while making clear that colonial boundary descriptions do not identify an exact modern watercourse or provide a complete Native account of the land.
introduction_title: A brook, a boundary, and a lived landscape
introduction_content: Mattuck names a brook recorded at East Moriches, but this listing does not claim an exact modern stream course. In his 1911 place-name study, William Wallace Tooker cited a Brookhaven history that described Mattuck as the eastern boundary of Watchogue, a neck forming the eastern part of East Moriches; Pomiches Creek marked the west. Tooker interpreted Mattuck from matt, “bad,” and -tuck, “a creek,” but immediately cautioned that the recorded form might abbreviate a longer term. His Watchogue entry says Governor Andros authorized Henry Taylor to buy south-shore land on October 1, 1677, and prints February 12, 1679, for Taylor, Thomas Willets, and Thomas Townsend's purchase of Watchogue from Mayhew. A separate Tooker entry quotes a 1680 deed in which John Mayhue described his kinsman Warishone as living on a small neck west of Watchogue. These records place the water name within a lived Native landscape of kinship and residence that colonial records describe through boundary and purchase language.
translation_content:
The name is interpreted as bad creek, from elements glossed as bad and creek. The history also leaves open the possibility that Mattuck is an abbreviated form of a longer term.

Why Place Names Matter

“The names of places on the landscape document layers of history.”

— Karen K. Gaul, Nanutset ch’u Q’udi Gu: Before Our Time and Now (2007), PDF page 99
whereintheworld_content: Map location note: the pin is placed in East Moriches near the likely eastern side of Watchogue neck to represent Mattuck Brook as a boundary stream; it is not an exact surveyed brook location.
